t: Rearrange String to Avoid Character Pair — Counting Partition
o: We need any permutation of s in which no x appears before a y — equivalently, every y comes before every x. Characters other than x and y are unconstrained. In Example 1 (s="aabc", x='a', y='c'), putting the single 'c' first satisfies the rule. In Example 3, x does not occur, so s itself is already valid. The simplest construction: emit all copies of y first, then everything else.
k: Only the relative order of x and y matters; all other characters can be dumped anywhere.
Placing all y's first and all remaining characters after trivially guarantees every y precedes every x.
Any valid permutation is accepted, so no optimization of the layout is required.

a.i: Build the answer in two passes: first append every character equal to y, then append every other character in original order. Since no x appears in the first block and no y appears in the second, the condition holds by construction.
s: Iterate over s and collect all characters equal to y into the result.
Iterate again and append every character that is not equal to y.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes over s.

a.n: Approach 2: Counting sort by custom key
a.i: Assign key 0 to y and key 1 to everything else, then stable-sort characters by key. This generalizes naturally if more precedence rules are added later, and produces an equally valid answer.
s: Map each character to 0 if it equals y, otherwise 1.
Stable sort the characters by this key.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by the sort.
a.sp: O(n) — for the character array / output.

w: Prefer Approach 1: it is linear, obviously correct, and needs no stability argument. Common mistakes: accidentally placing x before y by sorting alphabetically, or misreading the condition as "no y after x" (it is the same thing, but keep the direction straight). Edge cases: strings with no x or no y (any output works), and single-character strings. A follow-up might ask for the lexicographically smallest valid arrangement — then sort each block internally.
